claims.text: The effects of retirement savings policies on wealth accumulation depend on whether they change savings rates by active or passive choice.
Subsidies for retirement accounts primarily induce individuals to shift assets from taxable accounts to retirement accounts.
Each $1 of government expenditure on subsidies increases total saving by only 1 cent.
Policies that raise retirement contributions if individuals take no action, such as automatic employer contributions, increase wealth accumulation substantially.
Approximately 15% of individuals are active savers who respond to tax subsidies primarily by shifting assets across accounts.
Approximately 85% of individuals are passive savers who are unresponsive to subsidies but heavily influenced by automatic contributions made on their behalf.
Active savers tend to be wealthier than passive savers.
Active savers tend to be more financially sophisticated than passive savers.
Subsidies induce relatively few individuals to respond.
Subsidies generate substantial crowd-out conditional on response.
Subsidies do not increase the savings of passive individuals, who are least prepared for retirement.

evidence.description: Using 41 million observations on savings for the population of Denmark, the authors show that the effects of retirement savings policies on wealth accumulation depend on whether they change savings rates by active or passive choice.
Subsidies for retirement accounts, which rely on individuals to take an action to raise savings, primarily induce individuals to shift assets from taxable accounts to retirement accounts.
The authors estimate that each $1 of government expenditure on subsidies increases total saving by only 1 cent.
Policies that raise retirement contributions if individuals take no action—such as automatic employer contributions to retirement accounts—increase wealth accumulation substantially.
The authors estimate that approximately 15% of individuals are 'active savers' who respond to tax subsidies primarily by shifting assets across accounts.
The authors estimate that 85% of individuals are 'passive savers' who are unresponsive to subsidies but are instead heavily influenced by automatic contributions made on their behalf.
Empirical analysis indicates that active savers tend to be wealthier.
Empirical analysis indicates that active savers tend to be more financially sophisticated.
Automatic contributions are shown to be more effective than subsidies in part because subsidies induce relatively few individuals to respond.
Automatic contributions are shown to be more effective than subsidies in part because subsidies generate substantial crowd-out conditional on response.
Automatic contributions are shown to be more effective than subsidies in part because subsidies do not increase the savings of passive individuals, who are least prepared for retirement.

methodologies.name: Administrative Savings Data Analysis
methodologies.description: Analysis of population-level administrative observations to compare the effects of active-choice tax subsidies versus passive-choice automatic employer contributions on retirement savings and wealth accumulation.
datasets: Population savings records for Denmark (41 million observations)
